captions: Part five. How does the system find the
ten most similar memories, fast? Let's go inside
the vector search.
An embedding model maps text to a point
in space, fifteen hundred and thirty six numbers
long, where similar meanings land close together.
Closeness is measured with cosine similarity: the cosine
of the angle between two vectors. Same direction
gives one. Unrelated gives nearly zero.
Here, in a two dimensional sketch, the question,
where does Riya live, points almost the same
way as, lives in Bengaluru.
Cricket and vegetarian point elsewhere.
Rank by cosine, keep the top k, and
you have your candidates. The math is simple.
The hard part is doing it over millions
of vectors.
The naive approach compares the query with every
stored vector.
With a million memories of fifteen hundred and
thirty six dimensions, that's about one and a
half billion multiply-adds, for a single search.
Fine for a demo. Too slow for agents
answering in real time, across thousands of users.
So vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour indexes.
The most popular is HNSW.
HNSW stands for Hierarchical Navigable Small World.
Picture several layers of graphs. The bottom layer
contains every vector, each linked to its nearest
neighbours.
Each layer above keeps a random, much smaller
sample, like express lanes.
A search starts at the top, at a
fixed entry point. It greedily hops to whichever
neighbour is closer to the query, until no
neighbour improves.
Then it drops a layer, and continues from
there.
At the bottom, it keeps a candidate list
of size e f, and returns the best
k.
Instead of scanning every point, it visits only
a few dozen. The cost grows roughly with
the logarithm of the collection size.
How does a vector get into this structure?
When a new vector is inserted, it draws
a random top layer, using minus the log
of a uniform random number, scaled by one
over the log of M.
The result: the chance of reaching layer l
falls as M to the minus l.
With a million vectors and M of sixteen,
every vector is on layer zero. About sixty
two thousand reach layer one. Around thirty nine
hundred reach layer two. About two hundred and
forty four reach layer three. And only about
fifteen reach layer four.
At each layer, the new vector searches for
its nearest neighbours, and links to up to
M of them. That's why lookups take only
a handful of hops per layer.
Qdrant, Mem0's default store, exposes a few knobs.
M, the number of links per node: sixteen
by default. More links give better recall, but
use more memory.
e f construct, a hundred by default: how
many candidates to consider while building.
e f at search time, which by default
matches e f construct.
And payload filters, which apply the user and
agent scoping during the search itself, rather than
after it.
